terms.title: Arity
terms.summary: The number of arguments a function takes. From words like unary, binary, ternary, etc.
terms.body:
The number of arguments a function takes. From words like unary, binary, ternary, etc.

```js
const sum = (a, b) => a + b
// The arity of sum is 2 (binary)
const inc = a => a + 1
// The arity of inc is 1 (unary)
const zero = () => 0
// The arity of zero is 0 (nullary)
```

__Further reading__

* [Arity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arity) on Wikipedia

terms.title: Higher-Order Functions (HOF)
terms.summary: A function which takes a function as an argument and/or returns a function.
terms.body:
A function which takes a function as an argument and/or returns a function.

```js
const filter = (predicate, xs) => xs.filter(predicate)
```

```js
const is = (type) => (x) => Object(x) instanceof type
```

```js
filter(is(Number), [0, '1', 2, null]) // [0, 2]
```

codeBlocks.code: const filter = (predicate, xs) => xs.filter(predicate)
const is = (type) => (x) => Object(x) instanceof type
filter(is(Number), [0, '1', 2, null]) // [0, 2]

terms.title: Closure
terms.summary: A closure is a scope which captures local variables of a function for access even after the execution has moved out of the block in which it is defined. This allows the values in the closure to be accessed by returned functions.
terms.body:
A closure is a scope which captures local variables of a function for access even after the execution has moved out of the block in which it is defined.
This allows the values in the closure to be accessed by returned functions.

```js
const addTo = x => y => x + y
const addToFive = addTo(5)
addToFive(3) // => 8
```

In this case the `x` is retained in `addToFive`'s closure with the value `5`. `addToFive` can then be called with the `y`
to get back the sum.

__Further reading/Sources__
* [Lambda Vs Closure](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/220658/what-is-the-difference-between-a-closure-and-a-lambda)
* [JavaScript Closures highly voted discussion](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/111102/how-do-javascript-closures-work)

terms.title: Partial Application
terms.summary: Partially applying a function means creating a new function by pre-filling some of the arguments to the original function.

codeBlocks.code: const add1More = add3.bind(null, 2, 3) // (c) => 2 + 3 + c

terms.title: Currying
terms.summary: The process of converting a function that takes multiple arguments into a function that takes them one at a time.
terms.body:
The process of converting a function that takes multiple arguments into a function that takes them one at a time.

Each time the function is called it only accepts one argument and returns a function that takes one argument until all arguments are passed.

```js
const sum = (a, b) => a + b

const curriedSum = (a) => (b) => a + b

curriedSum(40)(2) // 42.

const add2 = curriedSum(2) // (b) => 2 + b

add2(10) // 12
```

codeBlocks.code:
const sum = (a, b) => a + b

const curriedSum = (a) => (b) => a + b

curriedSum(40)(2) // 42.

const add2 = curriedSum(2) // (b) => 2 + b

add2(10) // 12

terms.title: Auto Currying
terms.summary: Transforming a function that takes multiple arguments into one that if given less than its correct number of arguments returns a function that takes the rest. When the function gets the correct number of arguments it is then evaluated.
terms.body:
Transforming a function that takes multiple arguments into one that if given less than its correct number of arguments returns a function that takes the rest. When the function gets the correct number of arguments it is then evaluated.

Lodash & Ramda have a `curry` function that works this way.

```js
const add = (x, y) => x + y

const curriedAdd = _.curry(add)
curriedAdd(1, 2) // 3
curriedAdd(1) // (y) => 1 + y
curriedAdd(1)(2) // 3
```

__Further reading__
* [Favoring Curry](http://fr.umio.us/favoring-curry/)
* [Hey Underscore, You're Doing It Wrong!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m3svKOdZijA)

codeBlocks.code:
const add = (x, y) => x + y

const curriedAdd = _.curry(add)
curriedAdd(1, 2) // 3
curriedAdd(1) // (y) => 1 + y
curriedAdd(1)(2) // 3

furtherReading.title: Hey Underscore, You're Doing It Wrong!

terms.title: Function Composition
terms.summary: The act of putting two functions together to form a third function where the output of one function is the input of the other. This is one of the most important ideas of functional programming.
terms.body:
The act of putting two functions together to form a third function where the output of one function is the input of the other. This is one of the most important ideas of functional programming.

```js
const compose = (f, g) => (a) => f(g(a)) // Definition
const floorAndToString = compose((val) => val.toString(), Math.floor) // Usage
floorAndToString(121.212121) // '121'
```

codeBlocks.code:
const compose = (f, g) => (a) => f(g(a)) // Definition
const floorAndToString = compose((val) => val.toString(), Math.floor) // Usage
floorAndToString(121.212121) // '121'

terms.title: Continuation
terms.summary: At any given point in a program, the part of the code that's yet to be executed is known as a continuation.

terms.title: IO
terms.summary: A pure data structure that encapsulates a side effect. Instead of performing the effect immediately, IO wraps the action in a nullary function (thunk), allowing effectful operations to be transformed, chained, and composed as pure values without actually executing them until explicitly triggered.

terms.title: Trampoline
terms.summary: A mechanism that enables deep or mutually recursive functions to run without exceeding the maximum call stack limit.

terms.title: Thunk
terms.summary: A nullary function (a function taking zero arguments) that wraps an expression to delay its evaluation until called. Thunks are the fundamental mechanism for implementing lazy evaluation, trampolines, and deferred side effects.

terms.title: Algebraic Effects
terms.summary: A computational effect system that separates the invocation of an effect from its handling. Rather than coupling a function directly to its runtime environment, the function "performs" an effect operation (such as reading state, requesting configuration, or logging). An enclosing "handler" intercepts the performed effect and supplies the result, with the ability to resume or abort the computation—generalizing exceptions, async/await, and generators without requiring complex monad transformer stacks.

furtherReading.title: Algebraic Effects for the Rest of Us

terms.title: Pure Function
terms.summary: A function is pure if the return value is only determined by its input values, and does not produce side effects. The function must always return the same result when given the same input.
terms.body:
A function is pure if the return value is only determined by its input values, and does not produce side effects. The function must always return the same result when given the same input.

```js
const greet = (name) => `Hi, ${name}`

greet('Brianne') // 'Hi, Brianne'
```

As opposed to each of the following:

```js
window.name = 'Brianne'

const greet = () => `Hi, ${window.name}`

greet() // "Hi, Brianne"
```

The above example's output is based on data stored outside of the function...

```js
let greeting

const greet = (name) => {
  greeting = `Hi, ${name}`
}

greet('Brianne')
greeting // "Hi, Brianne"
```

... and this one modifies state outside of the function.

codeBlocks.code:
const greet = (name) => `Hi, ${name}`

greet('Brianne') // 'Hi, Brianne'

window.name = 'Brianne'

const greet = () => `Hi, ${window.name}`

greet() // "Hi, Brianne"

terms.title: Side effects
terms.summary: A function or expression is said to have a side effect if apart from returning a value, it interacts with (reads from or writes to) external mutable state.
terms.body:
A function or expression is said to have a side effect if apart from returning a value, it interacts with (reads from or writes to) external mutable state.

```js
const differentEveryTime = new Date()
```

```js
console.log('IO is a side effect!')
```

codeBlocks.code: const differentEveryTime = new Date()
console.log('IO is a side effect!')

terms.title: Idempotence
terms.summary: A function is idempotent if reapplying it to its result does not produce a different result.
terms.body:
A function is idempotent if reapplying it to its result does not produce a different result.

```js
Math.abs(Math.abs(10))
```

```js
sort(sort(sort([2, 1])))
```

codeBlocks.code: Math.abs(Math.abs(10))
sort(sort(sort([2, 1])))

terms.title: Point-Free Style
terms.summary: Writing functions where the definition does not explicitly identify the arguments used. This style usually requires currying or other Higher-Order functions. A.K.A Tacit programming.

terms.title: Predicate
terms.summary: A predicate is a function that returns true or false for a given value. A common use of a predicate is as the callback for array filter.
terms.body:
A predicate is a function that returns true or false for a given value. A common use of a predicate is as the callback for array filter.

```js
const predicate = (a) => a > 2

;[1, 2, 3, 4].filter(predicate) // [3, 4]
```

codeBlocks.code:
const predicate = (a) => a > 2

;[1, 2, 3, 4].filter(predicate) // [3, 4]

terms.title: Contracts
terms.summary: A contract specifies the obligations and guarantees of the behavior from a function or expression at runtime. This acts as a set of rules that are expected from the input and output of a function or expression, and errors are generally reported whenever a contract is violated.
terms.body:
A contract specifies the obligations and guarantees of the behavior from a function or expression at runtime. This acts as a set of rules that are expected from the input and output of a function or expression, and errors are generally reported whenever a contract is violated.

```js
// Define our contract : int -> boolean
const contract = (input) => {
  if (typeof input === 'number') return true
  throw new Error('Contract violated: expected int -> boolean')
}

const addOne = (num) => contract(num) && num + 1

addOne(2) // 3
addOne('some string') // Contract violated: expected int -> boolean
```

terms.title: Category
terms.summary: A category in category theory is a collection of objects and morphisms between them. In programming, typically types act as the objects and functions as morphisms.

terms.title: Semigroupoid
terms.summary: An algebraic structure with objects and morphisms that can be associatively composed, but does not guarantee the existence of an identity morphism for each object.

terms.title: Value
terms.summary: Anything that can be assigned to a variable.
terms.body:
Anything that can be assigned to a variable.

```js
5
Object.freeze({ name: 'John', age: 30 }) // The `freeze` function enforces immutability.
;(a) => a
;[1]
undefined
```

codeBlocks.code:
5
Object.freeze({ name: 'John', age: 30 }) // The `freeze` function enforces immutability.
;(a) => a
;[1]
undefined

terms.title: Constant
terms.summary: A variable that cannot be reassigned once defined.
terms.body:
A variable that cannot be reassigned once defined.

```js
const five = 5
const john = Object.freeze({ name: 'John', age: 30 })
```

Constants are [referentially transparent](#referential-transparency). That is, they can be replaced with the values that they represent without affecting the result.

With the above two constants the following expression will always return `true`.

```js
john.age + five === ({ name: 'John', age: 30 }).age + 5
```

codeBlocks.code:
const five = 5
const john = Object.freeze({ name: 'John', age: 30 })
john.age + five === ({ name: 'John', age: 30 }).age + 5

terms.title: Constant Function
terms.summary: A curried function that ignores its second argument:
terms.body:
A [curried](#currying) function that ignores its second argument:

```js
const constant = a => () => a

;[1, 2].map(constant(0)) // => [0, 0]
```

codeBlocks.code:
const constant = a => () => a

;[1, 2].map(constant(0)) // => [0, 0]

terms.title: Constant Functor
terms.summary: Object whose map doesn't transform the contents. See Functor.
terms.body:
Object whose `map` doesn't transform the contents. See [Functor](#functor).

```js
Constant(1).map(n => n + 1) // => Constant(1)
```

codeBlocks.code: Constant(1).map(n => n + 1) // => Constant(1)

terms.title: Constant Monad
terms.summary: Object whose chain doesn't transform the contents. See Monad.
terms.body:
Object whose `chain` doesn't transform the contents. See [Monad](#monad).

```js
Constant(1).chain(n => Constant(n + 1)) // => Constant(1)
```

codeBlocks.code: Constant(1).chain(n => Constant(n + 1)) // => Constant(1)

terms.title: Functor
terms.summary: An object that implements a map function that takes a function which is run on the contents of that object. A functor must adhere to two rules:
terms.body:
An object that implements a `map` function that takes a function which is run on the contents of that object. A functor must adhere to two rules:

__Preserves identity__

```js
object.map(x => x)
```

is equivalent to just `object`.

__Composable__

```js
object.map(x => g(f(x)))
```

is equivalent to

```js
object.map(f).map(g)
```

(`f`, `g` are arbitrary composable functions)

The reference implementation of [Option](#option) is a functor as it satisfies the rules:

```js
Some(1).map(x => x) // = Some(1)
```

and

```js
const f = x => x + 1
const g = x => x * 2

Some(1).map(x => g(f(x))) // = Some(4)
Some(1).map(f).map(g) // = Some(4)
```

codeBlocks.code: object.map(x => x)
object.map(x => g(f(x)))
object.map(f).map(g)
Some(1).map(x => x) // = Some(1)

const f = x => x + 1
const g = x => x * 2

Some(1).map(x => g(f(x))) // = Some(4)
Some(1).map(f).map(g) // = Some(4)

terms.title: Pointed Functor
terms.summary: An object with an of function that puts any single value into it.
terms.body:
An object with an `of` function that puts _any_ single value into it.

ES2015 adds `Array.of` making arrays a pointed functor.

```js
Array.of(1) // [1]
```

codeBlocks.code: Array.of(1) // [1]

terms.title: Lift
terms.summary: Lifting is when you take a value and put it into an object like a functor. If you lift a function into an Applicative Functor then you can make it work on values that are also in that functor.
terms.body:
Lifting is when you take a value and put it into an object like a [functor](#pointed-functor). If you lift a function into an [Applicative Functor](#applicative-functor) then you can make it work on values that are also in that functor.

Some implementations have a function called `lift`, or `liftA2` to make it easier to run functions on functors.

```js
const liftA2 = (f) => (a, b) => a.map(f).ap(b) // note it's `ap` and not `map`.

const mult = a => b => a * b

const liftedMult = liftA2(mult) // this function now works on functors like array

liftedMult([1, 2], [3]) // [3, 6]
liftA2(a => b => a + b)([1, 2], [30, 40]) // [31, 41, 32, 42]
```

Lifting a one-argument function and applying it does the same thing as `map`.

```js
const increment = (x) => x + 1

lift(increment)([2]) // [3]
;[2].map(increment) // [3]
```

Lifting simple values can be simply creating the object.

```js
Array.of(1) // => [1]
```

codeBlocks.code:
const liftA2 = (f) => (a, b) => a.map(f).ap(b) // note it's `ap` and not `map`.

const mult = a => b => a * b

const liftedMult = liftA2(mult) // this function now works on functors like array

liftedMult([1, 2], [3]) // [3, 6]
liftA2(a => b => a + b)([1, 2], [30, 40]) // [31, 41, 32, 42]

const increment = (x) => x + 1

lift(increment)([2]) // [3]
;[2].map(increment) // [3]

terms.title: Referential Transparency
terms.summary: An expression that can be replaced with its value without changing the behavior of the program is said to be referentially transparent.
terms.body:
An expression that can be replaced with its value without changing the
behavior of the program is said to be referentially transparent.

Given the function greet:

```js
const greet = () => 'Hello World!'
```

Any invocation of `greet()` can be replaced with `Hello World!` hence greet is
referentially transparent. This would be broken if greet depended on external
state like configuration or a database call. See also [Pure Function](#pure-function) and
[Equational Reasoning](#equational-reasoning).

codeBlocks.code: const greet = () => 'Hello World!'

terms.title: Equational Reasoning
terms.summary: When an application is composed of expressions and devoid of side effects, truths about the system can be derived from the parts. You can also be confident about details of your system without having to go through every function.
terms.body:
When an application is composed of expressions and devoid of side effects,
truths about the system can be derived from the parts. You can also be confident
about details of your system without having to go through every function.

```js
const grainToDogs = compose(chickenIntoDogs, grainIntoChicken)
const grainToCats = compose(dogsIntoCats, grainToDogs)
```

In the example above, if you know that `chickenIntoDogs` and `grainIntoChicken`
are [pure](#pure-function) then you know that the composition is pure. This can be taken further
when more is known about the functions (associative, commutative, idempotent, etc...).

codeBlocks.code:
const grainToDogs = compose(chickenIntoDogs, grainIntoChicken)
const grainToCats = compose(dogsIntoCats, grainToDogs)

terms.title: Memoization
terms.summary: An optimization technique that caches the return value of a function based on its input parameters. Memoization is only valid and safe for pure functions possessing referential transparency, because calling the function with identical arguments must always yield identical results without producing observable side effects.

terms.title: Lambda
terms.summary: An anonymous function that can be treated like a value.
terms.body:
An anonymous function that can be treated like a value.

```js
;(function (a) {
  return a + 1
})

;(a) => a + 1
```

Lambdas are often passed as arguments to Higher-Order functions:

```js
;[1, 2].map((a) => a + 1) // [2, 3]
```

You can assign a lambda to a variable:

```js
const add1 = (a) => a + 1
```

codeBlocks.code: const add1 = (a) => a + 1

terms.title: Lambda Calculus
terms.summary: A branch of mathematics that uses functions to create a universal model of computation.
terms.body: A branch of mathematics that uses functions to create a [universal model of computation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_calculus).

terms.title: Functional Combinator
terms.summary: A higher-order function, usually curried, which returns a new function changed in some way. Functional combinators are often used in Point-Free Style to write especially terse programs.

terms.title: Lazy evaluation
terms.summary: Lazy evaluation is a call-by-need evaluation mechanism that delays the evaluation of an expression until its value is needed. In functional languages, this allows for structures like infinite lists, which would not normally be available in an imperative language where the sequencing of commands is significant.

codeBlocks.code:
const randIter = rand()
randIter.next() // Each execution gives a random value, expression is evaluated on need.

terms.title: Monoid
terms.summary: An object with a function that "combines" that object with another of the same type (semigroup) which has an "identity" value.
terms.body:
An object with a function that "combines" that object with another of the same type (semigroup) which has an "identity" value.

One simple monoid is the addition of numbers:

```js
1 + 1 // 2
```

In this case number is the object and `+` is the function.

When any value is combined with the "identity" value the result must be the original value. The identity must also be commutative.

The identity value for addition is `0`.

```js
1 + 0 // 1
0 + 1 // 1
1 + 0 === 0 + 1
```

It's also required that the grouping of operations will not affect the result (associativity):

```js
1 + (2 + 3) === (1 + 2) + 3 // true
```

Array concatenation also forms a monoid:

```js
;[1, 2].concat([3, 4]) // [1, 2, 3, 4]
```

The identity value is empty array `[]`:

```js
;[1, 2].concat([]) // [1, 2]
```

As a counterexample, subtraction does not form a monoid because there is no commutative identity value:

```js
0 - 4 === 4 - 0 // false
```

terms.title: Monad
terms.summary: A monad is an object with of and chain functions. chain is like map except it un-nests the resulting nested object.

terms.title: Comonad
terms.summary: An object that has extract and extend functions.

codeBlocks.code: CoIdentity(1).extract() // 1
CoIdentity(1).extend((co) => co.extract() + 1) // CoIdentity(2)

terms.title: Kleisli Composition
terms.summary: An operation for composing two monad-returning functions (Kleisli Arrows) where they have compatible types. In Haskell this is the >=> operator.

terms.title: Free Monad
terms.summary: A Free Monad is a construction that builds a monad out of any functor without adding any domain-specific behavior. It cleanly separates the description of a program (an Abstract Syntax Tree of commands) from its execution (an interpreter that evaluates the AST).

terms.title: Monad Transformer
terms.summary: While functors and applicative functors compose naturally, monads do not compose generally without knowing their specific types. A Monad Transformer is a type constructor that takes an existing monad and produces a new monad with combined capabilities (such as combining error handling, asynchronous tasks, and state).

terms.title: Applicative Functor
terms.summary: An applicative functor is an object with an ap function. ap applies a function in the object to a value in another object of the same type.

codeBlocks.code: partiallyAppliedAdds.ap(arg2) // [5, 6, 7, 8]

terms.title: Bifunctor
terms.summary: A structure with two independent type parameters that can map over both of them simultaneously. A Bifunctor provides bimap, which takes two functions and maps the first over the first type parameter and the second over the second type parameter.
terms.body:
A structure with two independent type parameters that can map over both of them simultaneously. A Bifunctor provides `bimap`, which takes two functions and maps the first over the first type parameter and the second over the second type parameter.

```js
const Pair = (first, second) => ({
  first,
  second,
  bimap: (f, g) => Pair(f(first), g(second)),
  firstMap: (f) => Pair(f(first), second),
  secondMap: (g) => Pair(first, g(second))
})

const score = Pair('alice', 10)
score.bimap((name) => name.toUpperCase(), (points) => points * 2)
// Pair('ALICE', 20)
```

__Further reading__
* [Bifunctor](https://github.com/fantasyland/fantasy-land#bifunctor) in Fantasy Land

terms.title: Contravariant Functor
terms.summary: A structure similar to a functor, but whose transformation flows in the opposite direction. While a covariant functor transforms a producer F<A> into F<B> via (a -> b), a contravariant functor transforms a consumer F<A> into F<B> via (b -> a) using cmap (or contramap).

terms.title: Profunctor
terms.summary: A Profunctor is a bifunctor that is contravariant in its first argument and covariant in its second argument.

terms.title: Alternative
terms.summary: An applicative functor that also forms a monoid, providing a binary choice operator alt (often written <|>) and an identity element for failure recovery and fallback logic.

terms.title: Morphism
terms.summary: A relationship between objects within a category. In the context of functional programming all functions are morphisms.
terms.body: A relationship between objects within a [category](#category). In the context of functional programming all functions are morphisms.

terms.title: Homomorphism
terms.summary: A function where there is a structural property that is the same in the input as well as the output.
terms.body:
A function where there is a structural property that is the same in the input as well as the output.

For example, in a [Monoid](#monoid) homomorphism both the input and the output are monoids even if their types are different.

```js
// toList :: [number] -> string
const toList = (a) => a.join(', ')
```

`toList` is a homomorphism because:
* array is a monoid - has a `concat` operation and an identity value (`[]`),
* string is a monoid - has a `concat` operation and an identity value (`''`).

In this way, a homomorphism relates to whatever property you care about in the input and output of a transformation.

[Endomorphisms](#endomorphism) and [Isomorphisms](#isomorphism) are examples of homomorphisms.

__Further Reading__
* [Homomorphism | Learning Functional Programming in Go](https://subscription.packtpub.com/book/application-development/9781787281394/11/ch11lvl1sec90/homomorphism#:~:text=A%20homomorphism%20is%20a%20correspondence,pointing%20to%20it%20from%20A.)

codeBlocks.code:
// toList :: [number] -> string
const toList = (a) => a.join(', ')

furtherReading.title: Homomorphism | Learning Functional Programming in Go

terms.title: Endomorphism
terms.summary: A function where the input type is the same as the output. Since the types are identical, endomorphisms are also homomorphisms.

terms.title: Isomorphism
terms.summary: A morphism made of a pair of transformations between 2 types of objects that is structural in nature and no data is lost.

terms.title: Catamorphism
terms.summary: A function which deconstructs a structure into a single value. reduceRight is an example of a catamorphism for array structures.

terms.title: Anamorphism
terms.summary: A function that builds up a structure by repeatedly applying a function to its argument. unfold is an example which generates an array from a function and a seed value. This is the opposite of a catamorphism. You can think of this as an anamorphism builds up a structure and catamorphism breaks it down.

terms.title: Hylomorphism
terms.summary: The function which composes an anamorphism followed by a catamorphism.
terms.body:
The function which composes an [anamorphism](#anamorphism) followed by a [catamorphism](#catamorphism).

```js
const sumUpToX = (x) => sum(countDown(x))
sumUpToX(5) // 15
```

codeBlocks.code:
const sumUpToX = (x) => sum(countDown(x))
sumUpToX(5) // 15

terms.title: Paramorphism
terms.summary: A function just like reduceRight. However, there's a difference:

terms.title: Apomorphism
terms.summary: The opposite of paramorphism, just as anamorphism is the opposite of catamorphism. With paramorphism, you retain access to the accumulator and what has been accumulated, apomorphism lets you unfold with the potential to return early.
terms.body: The opposite of paramorphism, just as anamorphism is the opposite of catamorphism. With paramorphism, you retain access to the accumulator and what has been accumulated, apomorphism lets you `unfold` with the potential to return early.

terms.title: Natural Transformation
terms.summary: A structure-preserving mapping between two functors, transforming F<A> into G<A> without altering or inspecting the underlying value A.

terms.title: Setoid
terms.summary: An object that has an equals function which can be used to compare other objects of the same type.

terms.title: Semigroup
terms.summary: An object that has a concat function that combines it with another object of the same type.
terms.body:
An object that has a `concat` function that combines it with another object of the same type.

```js
;[1].concat([2]) // [1, 2]
```

terms.title: Foldable
terms.summary: An object that has a reduce function that applies a function against an accumulator and each element in the array (from left to right) to reduce it to a single value.
terms.body:
An object that has a `reduce` function that applies a function against an accumulator and each element in the array (from left to right) to reduce it to a single value.

```js
const sum = (list) => list.reduce((acc, val) => acc + val, 0)
sum([1, 2, 3]) // 6
```

codeBlocks.code:
const sum = (list) => list.reduce((acc, val) => acc + val, 0)
sum([1, 2, 3]) // 6

terms.title: Traversable
terms.summary: A Foldable and Functor that can turn a collection of wrapped values inside-out via sequence or traverse, transforming F<G<A>> into G<F<A>>.
terms.body:
A [Foldable](#foldable) and [Functor](#functor) that can turn a collection of wrapped values inside-out via `sequence` or `traverse`, transforming `F<G<A>>` into `G<F<A>>`.

This is commonly used to take a list of asynchronous operations or nullable values and pull the wrapper effect to the outside.

```js
// sequence transforms a list of Promises into a Promise of a list
// [Promise<1>, Promise<2>] -> Promise<[1, 2]>
const promiseSequence = (promises) =>
  promises.reduce(
    (acc, p) => acc.then((arr) => p.then((val) => [...arr, val])),
    Promise.resolve([])
  )

promiseSequence([
  Promise.resolve(1),
  Promise.resolve(2),
  Promise.resolve(3)
]).then(console.log) // [1, 2, 3]
```

__Further reading__
* [Traversable](https://github.com/fantasyland/fantasy-land#traversable) in Fantasy Land

terms.title: Lens
terms.summary: A lens is a structure (often an object or function) that pairs a getter and a non-mutating setter for some other data structure.

terms.title: Prism
terms.summary: An optic that focuses on a sub-case or variant of a sum type. Unlike a Lens, which always assumes the target field exists on a product structure, a Prism may fail to match because the target variant might not be present.
terms.body:
An optic that focuses on a sub-case or variant of a [sum type](#sum-type). Unlike a [Lens](#lens), which always assumes the target field exists on a product structure, a Prism may fail to match because the target variant might not be present.

A Prism consists of a `preview` function (which returns an [Option](#option) or null) and a `review` function (which reconstructs the whole data structure from the focused part).

```js
const Prism = (preview, review) => ({
  preview,
  review
})

// A prism focusing on numeric string values
const integerPrism = Prism(
  (str) => (/^-?\d+$/.test(str) ? Number(str) : null),
  (num) => String(num)
)

integerPrism.preview('42') // 42
integerPrism.preview('hello') // null
integerPrism.review(42) // '42'
```

__Further reading__
* [Optics / Prism](https://github.com/flunc/optics) on GitHub

terms.title: Iso
terms.summary: An optic that defines a lossless, reversible two-way mapping between two representations of the same information (s and a). An Iso consists of a to function (s -> a) and a from function (a -> s) such that from(to(x)) === x and to(from(y)) === y.
terms.body:
An optic that defines a lossless, reversible two-way mapping between two representations of the same information (`s` and `a`). An Iso consists of a `to` function (`s -> a`) and a `from` function (`a -> s`) such that `from(to(x)) === x` and `to(from(y)) === y`.

Isos form the foundation of reversible transformations like temperature conversions, coordinate systems, or encoding/decoding data structures.

```js
const Iso = (to, from) => ({
  to,
  from
})

// Conversion between Celsius and Fahrenheit
const tempIso = Iso(
  (c) => (c * 9) / 5 + 32, // to Fahrenheit
  (f) => ((f - 32) * 5) / 9 // from Fahrenheit
)

tempIso.to(100) // 212
tempIso.from(212) // 100
```

__Further reading__
* [Isomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphism) on Wikipedia
* [Optics / Iso](https://github.com/flunc/optics) on GitHub

terms.title: Traversal
terms.summary: An optic that focuses on zero, one, or multiple values (0..*) inside a data structure simultaneously.
terms.body:
An optic that focuses on zero, one, or multiple values (`0..*`) inside a data structure simultaneously.

While a [Lens](#lens) focuses on exactly 1 value and a [Prism](#prism) focuses on 0 or 1 value, a Traversal generalizes optics to collections, trees, or filtered subsets.

A traversal provides:
* `getAll`: extracts all focused values into an array.
* `modify`: immutably transforms every focused value using a mapping function.

```js
const Traversal = (getAll, modify) => ({
  getAll,
  modify
})

// Traversal focusing only on even numbers in an array:
const evenTraversal = Traversal(
  (arr) => arr.filter((n) => n % 2 === 0),
  (f, arr) => arr.map((n) => (n % 2 === 0 ? f(n) : n))
)

const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

evenTraversal.getAll(numbers) // [2, 4, 6]
evenTraversal.modify((n) => n * 10, numbers) // [1, 20, 3, 40, 5, 60]
```

__Further reading__
* [Optics - Traversals](https://github.com/calmm-js/partial.lenses#traversal)

terms.title: Algebraic data type
terms.summary: A composite type made from putting other types together. Two common classes of algebraic types are sum and product.
terms.body: A composite type made from putting other types together. Two common classes of algebraic types are [sum](#sum-type) and [product](#product-type).

terms.title: Sum type
terms.summary: A Sum type is the combination of two types together into another one. It is called sum because the number of possible values in the result type is the sum of the input types.

terms.title: Product type
terms.summary: A product type combines types together in a way you're probably more familiar with:

codeBlocks.code:
// point :: (Number, Number) -> {x: Number, y: Number}
const point = (x, y) => ({ x, y })

terms.title: Option
terms.summary: Option is a sum type with two cases often called Some and None.

terms.title: Either
terms.summary: A sum type with two cases, Left and Right. By convention, Right represents a successful computation and Left contains an error or failure reason ("right is right").

terms.title: Function
terms.summary: A function f :: A => B is an expression - often called arrow or lambda expression - with exactly one (immutable) parameter of type A and exactly one return value of type B. That value depends entirely on the argument, making functions context-independent, or referentially transparent. What is implied here is that a function must not produce any hidden side effects - a function is always pure, by definition. These properties make functions pleasant to work with: they are entirely deterministic and therefore predictable. Functions enable working with code as data, abstracting over behaviour:
terms.body:
A **function** `f :: A => B` is an expression - often called arrow or lambda expression - with **exactly one (immutable)** parameter of type `A` and **exactly one** return value of type `B`. That value depends entirely on the argument, making functions context-independent, or [referentially transparent](#referential-transparency). What is implied here is that a function must not produce any hidden [side effects](#side-effects) - a function is always [pure](#pure-function), by definition. These properties make functions pleasant to work with: they are entirely deterministic and therefore predictable. Functions enable working with code as data, abstracting over behaviour:

```js
// times2 :: Number -> Number
const times2 = n => n * 2

;[1, 2, 3].map(times2) // [2, 4, 6]
```

terms.title: Partial function
terms.summary: A partial function is a function which is not defined for all arguments - it might return an unexpected result or may never terminate. Partial functions add cognitive overhead, they are harder to reason about and can lead to runtime errors. Some examples:

terms.title: Dealing with partial functions
terms.summary: Partial functions are dangerous as they need to be treated with great caution. You might get an unexpected (wrong) result or run into runtime errors. Sometimes a partial function might not return at all. Being aware of and treating all these edge cases accordingly can become very tedious. Fortunately a partial function can be converted to a regular (or total) one. We can provide default values or use guards to deal with inputs for which the (previously) partial function is undefined. Utilizing the Option type, we can yield either Some(value) or None where we would otherwise have behaved unexpectedly:

terms.title: Total Function
terms.summary: A function which returns a valid result for all inputs defined in its type. This is as opposed to Partial Functions which may throw an error, return an unexpected result, or fail to terminate.
terms.body: A function which returns a valid result for all inputs defined in its type. This is as opposed to [Partial Functions](#partial-function) which may throw an error, return an unexpected result, or fail to terminate.

nodes.name: Arity
nodes.summary: The number of arguments a function takes. From words like unary, binary, ternary, etc.

nodes.name: Higher-Order Functions (HOF)
nodes.summary: A function which takes a function as an argument and/or returns a function.

nodes.name: Closure
nodes.summary: A closure is a scope which captures local variables of a function for access even after the execution has moved out of the block in which it is defined. This allows the values in the closure to be accessed by returned functions.

nodes.name: Partial Application
nodes.summary: Partially applying a function means creating a new function by pre-filling some of the arguments to the original function.

nodes.name: Currying
nodes.summary: The process of converting a function that takes multiple arguments into a function that takes them one at a time.

nodes.name: Auto Currying
nodes.summary: Transforming a function that takes multiple arguments into one that if given less than its correct number of arguments returns a function that takes the rest. When the function gets the correct number of arguments it is then evaluated.

nodes.name: Function Composition
nodes.summary: The act of putting two functions together to form a third function where the output of one function is the input of the other. This is one of the most important ideas of functional programming.

nodes.name: Continuation
nodes.summary: At any given point in a program, the part of the code that's yet to be executed is known as a continuation.

nodes.name: IO
nodes.summary: A pure data structure that encapsulates a side effect. Instead of performing the effect immediately, IO wraps the action in a nullary function (thunk), allowing effectful operations to be transformed, chained, and composed as pure values without actually executing them until explicitly triggered.

nodes.name: Trampoline
nodes.summary: A mechanism that enables deep or mutually recursive functions to run without exceeding the maximum call stack limit.

nodes.name: Thunk
nodes.summary: A nullary function (a function taking zero arguments) that wraps an expression to delay its evaluation until called. Thunks are the fundamental mechanism for implementing lazy evaluation, trampolines, and deferred side effects.

nodes.name: Algebraic Effects
nodes.summary: A computational effect system that separates the invocation of an effect from its handling. Rather than coupling a function directly to its runtime environment, the function "performs" an effect operation (such as reading state, requesting configuration, or logging). An enclosing "handler" intercepts the performed effect and supplies the result, with the ability to resume or abort the computation—generalizing exceptions, async/await, and generators without requiring complex monad transformer stacks.

nodes.name: Pure Function
nodes.summary: A function is pure if the return value is only determined by its input values, and does not produce side effects. The function must always return the same result when given the same input.

nodes.name: Side effects
nodes.summary: A function or expression is said to have a side effect if apart from returning a value, it interacts with (reads from or writes to) external mutable state.

nodes.name: Idempotence
nodes.summary: A function is idempotent if reapplying it to its result does not produce a different result.

nodes.name: Point-Free Style
nodes.summary: Writing functions where the definition does not explicitly identify the arguments used. This style usually requires currying or other Higher-Order functions. A.K.A Tacit programming.

nodes.name: Predicate
nodes.summary: A predicate is a function that returns true or false for a given value. A common use of a predicate is as the callback for array filter.

nodes.name: Contracts
nodes.summary: A contract specifies the obligations and guarantees of the behavior from a function or expression at runtime. This acts as a set of rules that are expected from the input and output of a function or expression, and errors are generally reported whenever a contract is violated.

nodes.name: Category
nodes.summary: A category in category theory is a collection of objects and morphisms between them. In programming, typically types act as the objects and functions as morphisms.

nodes.name: Semigroupoid
nodes.summary: An algebraic structure with objects and morphisms that can be associatively composed, but does not guarantee the existence of an identity morphism for each object.

nodes.name: Value
nodes.summary: Anything that can be assigned to a variable.

nodes.name: Constant
nodes.summary: A variable that cannot be reassigned once defined.

nodes.name: Constant Function
nodes.summary: A curried function that ignores its second argument:

nodes.name: Constant Functor
nodes.summary: Object whose map doesn't transform the contents. See Functor.

nodes.name: Constant Monad
nodes.summary: Object whose chain doesn't transform the contents. See Monad.

nodes.name: Functor
nodes.summary: An object that implements a map function that takes a function which is run on the contents of that object. A functor must adhere to two rules:

nodes.name: Pointed Functor
nodes.summary: An object with an of function that puts any single value into it.

nodes.name: Lift
nodes.summary: Lifting is when you take a value and put it into an object like a functor. If you lift a function into an Applicative Functor then you can make it work on values that are also in that functor.

nodes.name: Referential Transparency
nodes.summary: An expression that can be replaced with its value without changing the behavior of the program is said to be referentially transparent.

nodes.name: Equational Reasoning
nodes.summary: When an application is composed of expressions and devoid of side effects, truths about the system can be derived from the parts. You can also be confident about details of your system without having to go through every function.

nodes.name: Memoization
nodes.summary: An optimization technique that caches the return value of a function based on its input parameters. Memoization is only valid and safe for pure functions possessing referential transparency, because calling the function with identical arguments must always yield identical results without producing observable side effects.

nodes.name: Lambda
nodes.summary: An anonymous function that can be treated like a value.

nodes.name: Lambda Calculus
nodes.summary: A branch of mathematics that uses functions to create a universal model of computation.

nodes.name: Functional Combinator
nodes.summary: A higher-order function, usually curried, which returns a new function changed in some way. Functional combinators are often used in Point-Free Style to write especially terse programs.

nodes.name: Lazy evaluation
nodes.summary: Lazy evaluation is a call-by-need evaluation mechanism that delays the evaluation of an expression until its value is needed. In functional languages, this allows for structures like infinite lists, which would not normally be available in an imperative language where the sequencing of commands is significant.

nodes.name: Monoid
nodes.summary: An object with a function that "combines" that object with another of the same type (semigroup) which has an "identity" value.

nodes.name: Monad
nodes.summary: A monad is an object with of and chain functions. chain is like map except it un-nests the resulting nested object.

nodes.name: Comonad
nodes.summary: An object that has extract and extend functions.

nodes.name: Kleisli Composition
nodes.summary: An operation for composing two monad-returning functions (Kleisli Arrows) where they have compatible types. In Haskell this is the >=> operator.

nodes.name: Free Monad
nodes.summary: A Free Monad is a construction that builds a monad out of any functor without adding any domain-specific behavior. It cleanly separates the description of a program (an Abstract Syntax Tree of commands) from its execution (an interpreter that evaluates the AST).

nodes.name: Monad Transformer
nodes.summary: While functors and applicative functors compose naturally, monads do not compose generally without knowing their specific types. A Monad Transformer is a type constructor that takes an existing monad and produces a new monad with combined capabilities (such as combining error handling, asynchronous tasks, and state).

nodes.name: Applicative Functor
nodes.summary: An applicative functor is an object with an ap function. ap applies a function in the object to a value in another object of the same type.

nodes.name: Bifunctor
nodes.summary: A structure with two independent type parameters that can map over both of them simultaneously. A Bifunctor provides bimap, which takes two functions and maps the first over the first type parameter and the second over the second type parameter.

nodes.name: Contravariant Functor
nodes.summary: A structure similar to a functor, but whose transformation flows in the opposite direction. While a covariant functor transforms a producer F<A> into F<B> via (a -> b), a contravariant functor transforms a consumer F<A> into F<B> via (b -> a) using cmap (or contramap).

nodes.name: Profunctor
nodes.summary: A Profunctor is a bifunctor that is contravariant in its first argument and covariant in its second argument.

nodes.name: Alternative
nodes.summary: An applicative functor that also forms a monoid, providing a binary choice operator alt (often written <|>) and an identity element for failure recovery and fallback logic.

nodes.name: Morphism
nodes.summary: A relationship between objects within a category. In the context of functional programming all functions are morphisms.

nodes.name: Homomorphism
nodes.summary: A function where there is a structural property that is the same in the input as well as the output.

nodes.name: Endomorphism
nodes.summary: A function where the input type is the same as the output. Since the types are identical, endomorphisms are also homomorphisms.

nodes.name: Isomorphism
nodes.summary: A morphism made of a pair of transformations between 2 types of objects that is structural in nature and no data is lost.

nodes.name: Catamorphism
nodes.summary: A function which deconstructs a structure into a single value. reduceRight is an example of a catamorphism for array structures.

nodes.name: Anamorphism
nodes.summary: A function that builds up a structure by repeatedly applying a function to its argument. unfold is an example which generates an array from a function and a seed value. This is the opposite of a catamorphism. You can think of this as an anamorphism builds up a structure and catamorphism breaks it down.

nodes.name: Hylomorphism
nodes.summary: The function which composes an anamorphism followed by a catamorphism.
